readings.title: What general anaesthetic reveals about our brains
body: 19 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Jasmin Fox-Skelly How general anaesthetics work is still not fully understood, but they are revealing clues about the nature of consciousness. In 1797, the British naval commander Admiral Horatio Nelson had his right arm amputated. The operation saved his life. But according to legend the only anaesthetic he was offered was a swig of rum .  For the majority of human history, even the removal of limbs was done on patients who were fully awake. The introduction of general anaesthetics in 1846 was game-changing. Now consciousness could be temporarily switched off anytime, anywhere, in anyone. Nelson could have skipped the amputation but still turned up for breakfast the next day.  Today there are over 350 million surgeries performed under general anaesthesia every year. But how these mysterious medicines put us to sleep is still not entirely clear. Now emerging clues are teaching scientists about the fundamental workings of our brains. They're even hinting at the origins of consciousness itself. There are several categories of anaesthetics . Some work by blocking pain directly, while others make you sleepy and relaxed. General anaesthetics go one step further. These drugs make you unconscious, so you have no awareness whatsoever of what is going on.   There are a whole plethora of anaesthetics which can induce a state of unconsciousness. These range from seemingly inert gases such as xenon, which are rarely used in practice, to propofol, which is the most widely and commonly used general anaesthetic. General anaesthetics can have widely different chemical structures. In each case, the overall effect is to interfere with the communication of nerve cells in the brain, preventing them from talking to each other. What is clear from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans is that there is a global reduction in brain activity . However, exactly how this results in a patient being put to sleep is less well understood. For one thing, it's not yet clear whether the state of unconsciousness induced by anaesthetics requires the total shutdown of the whole brain. Or perhaps certain regions are more important than others. "Even if the whole brain shuts down, because it [the brain] is so interconnected it's very hard to dissect out what triggered the global shutdown," says Nick Franks, professor of biophysics and anaesthetics at Imperial College London, UK. "If you look at brain scans, it's clear there are certain regions that are more sensitive that shut down first, and that begs the question whether these then trigger a global shutdown."  Franks points to the thalamus , an egg-shaped structure deep in the brain that acts as a central hub between brain regions. This area appears to power down first when someone is given a general anaesthetic. The thalamus plays a crucial role in initiating and maintaining sleep, among other things. So do anaesthetics work by "hijacking" the brain's natural sleep circuitry? "If you anaesthetise an animal and then stimulate a very selective part of the thalamus, you can wake the animal up ," says Franks. "Studies also show that [some] people in a coma can be woken up by thalamic stimulation . So it's a critical area for arousal." However, more studies are needed to find out if this is what's going on. Other scientists believe that the cerebral cortex – the brain's outer wrinkly layer – is the main "home of consciousness" and therefore must be where anaesthetics exert their main effects. But there are other brain regions implicated too. For example, the frontal and parietal lobes . The former sits just behind your forehead, and is responsible for many higher-level activities such as critical thinking. The latter sits further back and is involved in processing sensory information, such as touch. But there are emerging clues that our brains might be capable of an in-between state of consciousness – one which is neither asleep nor awake.  For most people, being "put under" means losing total consciousness and therefore all memory of events. However, that isn't the case for everyone. An estimated one in 15,000 patients undergoing surgery can remember aspects of their surgery after waking, a phenomenon known as accidental awareness. Jaideep Pandit, a consultant anaesthetist at the Oxford University Hospitals, believes that such individuals are experiencing a "third state" of consciousness somewhere between sleeping and waking, or consciousness and unconsciousness. In tests, Pandit gave patients an anaesthetic along with a muscle relaxant, but used a tourniquet to prevent the muscle relaxant from paralysing the forearm. This allowed unconscious patients to move their hand if they so wished. He found that one third of patients were able to squeeze the experimenter's fingers on command, despite not showing any signs of being awake or in pain during surgery. According to Pandit, this suggests there is a third level of consciousness.  The so-called "hard problem" of consciousness remains one of the great unsolved mysteries of science. But looking at what's different when you lose this ability is helping to unlock its secrets. While regular sleep also involves a loss of consciousness, general anaesthetics allow it to be switched off at any moment, so they make it easier to study.   Take the uniqueness of our conscious experiences. It's generally accepted that each person or animal's conscious experience is entirely subjective and special to them.  Andrea Luppi, a neuroscientist at the University of Cambridge investigated if general anaesthetics can shed light on how this works. He looked at the brains of people under general anaesthesia using functional MRI scans. This technology can record blood flow in the brain, to see what impact the drugs have. Luppi was particularly interested in functional connectivity – a measure of how well different regions of the brain communicate and coordinate their activity. Normally, this type of neural activity follows a pattern that is so unique that it can act like a "fingerprint" to identity a person. More like this:  •  How to minimise air pollution when exercising   •  How allergies can develop in later life •  Here ’ s how to catch up on sleep, the right way However, Luppi and colleagues found that, under anaesthesia, individual brains became less "unique" and more similar to one another. Intriguingly, the anaesthetised human brain also became less distinguishable from the brains of other primates, suggesting that the regions of the human brain that are most affected by anaesthesia are those that are most evolutionarily recent. Luppi believes that a key signature of anaesthesia is that it stops disparate regions of the brain from talking to one another. During wakefulness, regions can interact even if they are not directly connected. However, this is very rare in the anaesthetised brain, where only regions that are directly linked to one another appear to "talk".  "During wakefulness, the stream of consciousness guides the sequence of brain patterns that we visit," Luppi wrote in a 2024 commentary . Instead, under anaesthesia brain activity is rudderless, he explained. Luppi's findings fit with the idea that consciousness does not result from activity in a specific brain region. Instead, it's a network – it emerges from the coordination of different hubs. Like shutting down a government by crashing a country's communications systems.  Luppi also believes that general anaesthetics could shine a light on how psychedelics such as LSD and psilocybin ("magic mushrooms") alter consciousness. While anaesthetics dampen communication between different brain regions, psychedelics appear to do the opposite – they induce the brain to open new lines of communication. Ultimately though, there's still a lot to learn about where consciousness resides in the human brain. "Our understanding of consciousness is pretty rudimentary," says Boris Heifets, associate professor of anaesthesiology, perioperative and pain medicine at Stanford University, California. "So I think if you can find someone to explain how conscious experience works, please let me know. I would love to talk to them." * All content within this article is provided for general information only, and should not be treated as a substitute for the medical advice of health care professionals. -- For trusted insights on health and wellbeing, sign up to the Health Fix newsletter by senior health correspondent Melissa Hogenboom who also writes the Live Well For Longer and Six Steps to Calm courses.  For more science, technology, environment and health stories from the BBC, follow us on  Facebook and Instagram . ##段落
19小时前 分享 收藏 在Google上添加为偏好 Jasmin Fox-Skelly 全身麻醉的工作原理至今仍未完全被理解，但它们正在揭示关于意识本质的线索。1797年，英国海军指挥官霍雷肖·纳尔逊上将的右臂被截肢。手术救了他的命。但据传说，唯一给他用的麻醉剂就是一大口朗姆酒。在人类历史的大部分时间里，即使是截肢手术也是在完全清醒的患者身上进行的。1846年全身麻醉的引入改变了这一切。现在，意识可以在任何时候、任何地点、任何人身上被暂时关闭。纳尔逊本可以跳过截肢手术，但第二天仍能正常出现在早餐桌前。如今，每年有超过3.5亿台手术在全身麻醉下进行。但这些神秘的药物究竟如何让我们入睡，仍不完全清楚。如今浮现的线索正在教科学家了解我们大脑的基本运作方式。它们甚至暗示了意识本身的起源。麻醉剂有几大类。有些通过直接阻断疼痛来起作用，而另一些则让你昏昏欲睡、放松下来。全身麻醉则更进一步。这些药物使你失去意识，因此你对正在发生的一切毫无感知。

##段落
有各种各样的麻醉剂可以诱导无意识状态。从实践中很少使用的看似惰性的气体如氙气，到丙泊酚——这是最广泛和最常用的全身麻醉剂。全身麻醉剂可以具有截然不同的化学结构。在每种情况下，总体效果都是干扰大脑中神经细胞之间的通信，阻止它们相互“交谈”。从磁共振成像（MRI）扫描中可以清楚地看到，大脑活动会全面减少。然而，这究竟如何导致患者被麻醉入睡，则不太清楚。首先，目前尚不清楚麻醉剂诱导的无意识状态是否需要整个大脑完全关闭。或者也许某些区域比其他区域更重要。“即使整个大脑关闭了，由于它（大脑）是如此相互连接，很难剖析出是什么触发了全局关闭，”英国伦敦帝国理工学院生物物理学与麻醉学教授尼克·弗兰克斯说。“如果你看脑部扫描，很明显有些区域更敏感，会先关闭，这就引出了一个问题：这些区域是否会进而触发全局关闭。”弗兰克斯指出丘脑——大脑深处一个蛋形结构，充当大脑各区域之间的中枢枢纽。当一个人被麻醉时，这个区域似乎最先关闭。

##段落
全身麻醉。丘脑在启动和维持睡眠等方面起着至关重要的作用。那么麻醉剂是否通过“劫持”大脑的自然睡眠回路来发挥作用呢？“如果你给动物实施麻醉，然后刺激丘脑中一个非常特定的部位，你可以让动物醒来，”弗兰克斯说。“研究还表明，[一些]处于昏迷状态的人可以通过丘脑刺激被唤醒。所以这是唤醒的关键区域。”然而，还需要更多研究来确定这是否就是实际发生的情况。其他科学家认为，大脑皮层——大脑外层布满皱纹的那一层——是主要的“意识之家”，因此必定是麻醉剂发挥主要作用的地方。但还有其他脑区也牵涉其中。例如，额叶和顶叶。前者位于前额正后方，负责许多高级活动，如批判性思维。后者位于更靠后的位置，参与处理触觉等感觉信息。但新出现的线索表明，我们的大脑可能能够处于一种介于两者之间的意识状态——既非睡眠也非清醒。对大多数人来说，被“麻醉”意味着完全失去意识，因此也失去对所有事件的记忆。然而，并非每个人都如此。据估计，每15,000名接受手术的患者中就有1名能在醒来后回忆起手术的某些方面，这种现象被称为意外觉醒。牛津大学医院的顾问麻醉师杰迪普·潘迪特认为，这类人正在经历一种介于睡眠与清醒之间、或意识与无意识之间的“第三状态”意识。在测试中，潘迪特给患者施行麻醉并配合肌肉松弛剂，但使用止血带阻止肌肉松弛剂麻痹前臂。这使得无意识的患者如果愿意的话可以移动他们的手。他发现三分之一的患者能够按指令捏实验者的手指，尽管他们在手术期间没有表现出任何清醒或疼痛的迹象。据潘迪特说，这表明存在第三层次的意识。所谓的意识“难问题”仍然是科学上最大的未解之谜之一。但研究当你失去这种能力时有什么不同，正在帮助揭开它的秘密。虽然正常睡眠也涉及意识的丧失，但全身麻醉允许意识在任何时刻被关闭，因此使研究变得更加容易。以我们意识体验的独特性为例。人们普遍认为，每个人或动物的意识体验完全是主观的，且对他们而言是独特的。剑桥大学的神经科学家安德烈亚·卢皮研究了全身麻醉是否

##段落
全身麻醉下的大脑活动可以揭示意识的工作原理。卢皮利用功能性核磁共振成像扫描观察了全身麻醉下人们的大脑。这项技术可以记录大脑中的血流情况，以了解药物的影响。卢皮对功能连接性尤其感兴趣——这是衡量大脑不同区域沟通和协调活动程度的指标。正常情况下，这种神经活动遵循一种极为独特的模式，甚至可以像“指纹”一样用来识别一个人。更多相关内容：• 运动时如何尽量减少空气污染的影响 • 过敏如何在晚年出现 • 以下是正确补觉的方法。然而，卢皮及其同事发现，在麻醉状态下，个体大脑变得不那么“独特”，彼此之间更加相似。有趣的是，被麻醉的人脑也变得更难与其他灵长类动物的大脑区分开来，这表明人脑中最受麻醉影响的区域，正是进化上最新的区域。卢皮认为，麻醉的一个关键特征是他阻断了大脑不同区域之间的交流。在清醒状态下，即使区域之间没有直接连接，它们也可以相互作用。然而，在被麻醉的大脑中，这种情况非常罕见，似乎只有彼此直接相连的区域才会“交谈”。

##段落
卢皮在2024年的一篇评论中写道：“在清醒状态下，意识流引导着我们经历一系列大脑模式。”他解释说，相反，在麻醉状态下，大脑活动失去了方向。卢皮的发现与这样一种观点相符：意识并非源于某个特定大脑区域的活动。相反，它是一个网络——它从不同枢纽的协调中涌现出来。就像通过摧毁一个国家的通信系统来让政府停摆一样。卢皮还认为，全身麻醉剂可以帮助揭示LSD和裸盖菇素（“神奇蘑菇”）等致幻剂如何改变意识。麻醉剂抑制大脑不同区域之间的沟通，而致幻剂似乎恰恰相反——它们诱导大脑开辟新的沟通线路。不过，归根结底，关于意识存在于人脑何处，仍有很多东西需要了解。加利福尼亚州斯坦福大学麻醉学、围手术期和疼痛医学副教授鲍里斯·海费茨说：“我们对意识的理解还相当初步。所以我想，如果你能找到一个人解释意识体验是如何运作的，请告诉我。我很想和他谈谈。”

##段落
* 本文中的所有内容仅供一般信息参考，不应被视为医疗保健专业人员医疗建议的替代品。

readings.title: Trump’s new arch plan: snipers and drones
body: Politics / Donald Trump / The Logoff Trump’s new arch plan: snipers and drones If you give the president his national security ballroom, he’s going to ask for his national security arch. by Cameron Peters Sep 21, 2026, 10:10 PM UTC Gift White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt shows an artist’s rendering of Donald Trump’s planned triumphal arch during a press briefing on April 15, 2026. Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images Cameron Peters is a staff editor at Vox. This story appeared in The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life. Subscribe here . Welcome to The Logoff: President Donald Trump’s proposed triumphal arch is going in a new direction: drone port and sniper platform. What’s happening? Trump has been pushing to build a 250-foot-tall “triumphal arch” near the National Mall since at least this January . Relative to some of his other projects, however, it’s been slow going, and now he has a new plan. Trump announced the updated design in a Sunday morning post, writing, “At the strong request of the United States Military, and for National Security purposes, I have agreed to convert” the arch into “a top grade Military Complex/Triumphal Arch.” In addition to drones, Trump said, the new arch will have “snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage.” Really? Maybe. We don’t yet know if this version of the arch will happen, or even if the military actually requested it. For that matter, we don’t know if the arch will get built at all — though the administration appears prepared to move forward, despite a National Park Service determination that the arch would harm nearby historical sites , including the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. What’s the big picture? Trump’s plan for a “Military Complex/Triumphal Arch” sounds an awful lot like his “Ballroom/Military Complex,” which got a stamp of approval from the Supreme Court last month after multiple lower courts ruled against its construction without permission from Congress (which Trump also does not have for his arch). Like the arch, the ballroom acquired its “military complex” label after running into obstacles (though unlike the arch, there’s a clear connection: The ballroom does in fact sit on top of a secure bunker). The unifying theme, though, is Trump’s instinct to reach for “national security” as a cudgel whenever he’s thwarted. He also accused the media of being a “threat to our National Security” on Monday amid backlash to his press ban . Hi readers — I could not have been more thrilled to read this story from DC’s Capital Weather team this morning declaring the start of fall and some much-needed cooler weather. I hope you’re getting the same, wherever you are. Plus, it’s September 21 — don’t miss this now-venerable NPR story on the history of the Earth, Wind & Fire hit “September” and why it continues to resonate. Have a great evening, and we’ll see you tomorrow! ##段落
政治 / 唐纳德·特朗普 / The Logoff 特朗普的新拱门计划：狙击手与无人机 如果你给了总统他的国家安全舞厅，他就会接着要他的国家安全拱门。 作者：卡梅伦·彼得斯 2026年9月21日，晚上10:10 UTC 赠阅 白宫新闻秘书卡罗琳·莱维特在2026年4月15日的新闻发布会上展示唐纳德·特朗普计划中的凯旋门的艺术效果图。Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images 卡梅伦·彼得斯是Vox的特约编辑。本文发表于《The Logoff》，这是一份每日通讯，帮助你在不让政治新闻占据生活的情况下了解特朗普政府的动态。点此订阅。

##段落
欢迎来到《The Logoff》：唐纳德·特朗普总统拟建的凯旋门正朝着一个新方向发展：无人机停机坪与狙击平台。 发生了什么？ 至少从今年1月起，特朗普就一直在推动在国家广场附近建造一座250英尺高的“凯旋门”。然而，与他其他一些项目相比，这个项目进展缓慢，如今他又有了新计划。特朗普在周日早间的一则帖子中宣布了更新后的设计，写道：“应美国军方的强烈要求，并为国家安全目的，我已同意”将该拱门改建为“一座顶级军事综合体/凯旋门”。特朗普表示，除了无人机，新拱门还将在“屋顶和广场区域部署狙击手，并额外储存和持有大量狙击弹药。”

##段落
真的吗？ 也许吧。我们尚不清楚这个版本的拱门是否会落地，甚至不清楚军方是否真的提出过这一要求。就此而言，我们也不知道这座拱门究竟会不会建成——尽管政府似乎已准备推进，即便国家公园管理局认定该拱门会损害附近的历史遗址，包括林肯纪念堂和阿灵顿国家公墓。

##段落
大局是什么？ 特朗普的“军事综合体/凯旋门”计划听起来非常像他的“舞厅/军事综合体”——在上个月多家下级法院裁定其未经国会批准不得施工（特朗普的拱门同样没有获得国会批准）之后，最高法院对后者予以放行。与拱门一样，舞厅也是在遭遇障碍后才获得了“军事综合体”的标签（不过与拱门不同的是，这里存在明确的关联：舞厅确实建在一座安全地堡之上）。然而，贯穿其中的共同主题是：每当特朗普受挫时，他都有诉诸“国家安全”作为大棒的本能。周一，在因其新闻禁令引发反弹之际，他还指责媒体是“对我们国家安全的威胁”。

readings.title: How to minimise air pollution while exercising
body: 19 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Melissa Hogenboom In general, the benefits of exercise outweigh the risks from air pollution. But there are steps we can take to minimise our exposure. I was waiting to cross the road during a recent morning run when a van pulled up beside me. I couldn't help but inhale a thick plume of exhaust smoke. As a keen cyclist and runner living in London this can be hard to avoid. Active travel is built into my commute, so I'm often stuck behind traffic while I wait for lights to change. As I cough away the latest wave of polluted air, I often wonder: is exercising on polluted roads doing me more harm than good? Here's everything you need to know about the risks and benefits, as well as how to best protect yourself when exercising in urban environments.  ' s in the air you ' re breathing?   It's well known that air pollution  is linked to chronic health conditions including heart disease, respiratory issues , cancer as well as a higher risk of an early death . According to the World Health Organization , 99% of the global population breathes in polluted air, leading to 6.7 million premature deaths per year.  Air pollution affects pretty much all the organs of your body , says Audrey de Nazelle, an associate professor at Imperial College London who researches the effects of pollution on exercise. "We used to think it was just respiratory disease, but it's also [linked to] cardiovascular disease, diabetes, cognitive function and reproductive impacts ," she says. One major concern is PM 2.5, tiny particles which measure just 2.5 micrometres across. These fine specks are around 30 times smaller than the width of a human hair. They are released directly into the air from traffic, and can penetrate deep into our lungs, crossing into our bloodstream and travelling throughout the body.  Over time, this particle accumulation can affect the brain. In a 2025 review looking at 51 studies, a team analysed data from over 29 million people and found a link between three types of air pollution and an increased risk of Parkinson's disease. One of these were PM 2.5. "When the particles are this small, they can cross the blood brain barrier, cause damage to the vessels and the barrier, but also end up in your brain," says Haneen Khreis, an epidemiologist at the University of Cambridge and a co-author of the study.  But there are other pollutants, too. While exercising along busy roads or in cities, we will be breathing in nitrogen dioxide , which was also found by the review to increase the risk of Parkinson's Disease. Nitrogen dioxide is also thought to cause lung inflammation. In the longer term, it can impair how our lungs develop and function. Then there's sulphur dioxide, ammonia, carbon monoxide and even ground-level ozone.  When we run, cycle or exercise vigorously, we breathe faster and more deeply. That means we tend to inhale more polluted air when running compared to walking. When covering the same distance, people exercising at a higher intensity receive a larger dose of toxic particles entering into their lungs. But perhaps surprisingly, sitting in a car doesn't completely shield you from air pollution either. "Personal exposures when you're on a bike are actually lower than if you're sitting in a car ," says Rudy Sinharay, a consultant respiratory physician and lung cancer specialist at Imperial College London NHS Trust. "Whereas when you're cycling, you tend to be moving a bit more. There's a bit more air blowing." And it's not just traffic, as underground transport in cities such as London and New York can contain high concentrations of fine particles, much of them metal-rich dust generated by the friction of wheels, rails and brakes. "The good news is that the benefits that you get from exercising in polluted cities outweigh the risks," says de Nazelle. In fact, the exercise itself may be protecting our bodies from the pollution, she says. For a 2016 study , de Nazelle and colleagues looked into exactly this. In a modelling study, they estimated that the health gains of walking and cycling outweigh the harms of dirty air. Only at exceptionally high pollution levels, such as those found in some of the world's most polluted cities like Delhi, India, do the risks begin to approach or exceed the benefits of prolonged exercise. And even in polluted areas, exercise reduces the risk of an early death.  A recent review paper found that exercising in air polluted environments was associated with a 26% reduction in mortality risk, compared with inactivity. As can be expected, exercising in cleaner air was found to be preferrable and had a higher reduction of 31%. For those living in urban environments, this should be encouraging, says de Nazelle. However, the benefits of exercising outdoors may not always outweigh the risks of air pollution – it's important to factor in your own medical circumstances. Those with preexisting health conditions , such as asthma or cardiovascular disease, should be more cautious.  Other research has found that exercise still improves lung function and lowers blood pressure in polluted areas. It can also counteract some of the cognitive impacts of pollution.   However, how polluted the air you're breathing also makes a big difference. In 2018, Sinharay and colleagues recruited healthy volunteers as well as older adults with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or coronary heart disease for a study. Participants were asked to take a two-hour walk in either a park or along a busy London street.  The team found that after only two hours, those walking in an area with cleaner air showed improved lung and blood vessel function. Those who walked in the area with high levels of pollution showed smaller benefits. In people with COPD, pollution exposure was associated with worse symptoms.  In other words, exercise offsets many of the harms of pollution, but the reverse is also true: heavy pollution reduces the protective effects that exercise provides. It even blunts the cognitive benefits of exercise. So for the most part the benefits outweigh the risks, but exercising in polluted air is still not ideal.  For those of us who live in a busy city, we can't simply uproot ourselves to the countryside for a jog. But the next best option is to find the greenest or least congested area around us. For instance, I have the option to cycle along a road with less traffic on my morning commute, but it does take a few minutes longer. Research shows that moving one or two streets away from heavy traffic slashes your pollution exposure by 20% to 30%, says de Nazelle . And if you can take side streets, even better. One study found that opting for side streets instead of busy routes cut exposure by 50%. More like this: •   How to exercise safely in hot weather •  Five minutes of exercise a day could help millions of people live longer •  How weight lifting can help you stay healthier as you age If possible, it's also a good idea to avoid rush hour. Cars sitting still in traffic create " pollution hotspots " says Khreis. Similarly, watch out for peaks of ozone during hot sunny afternoons, she advises. She explains that this potent chemical tends to form when it's really hot and there's abundant sunlight. Combining these factors with the air pollution at rush hour exacerbates the problem.    Finally, it might help to monitor local air quality pollution indexes . These can tell you the levels in your area on any given day. Sinharay advises that on days with higher air pollution, exercising indoors or in parks is a better option.  The bigger picture though, says Khreis, is that policy change will make a more meaningful impact beyond what we do on an individual level. "It's very much a systemic issue. While those personal choices can help us reduce our individual exposures, the most effective protection is going to be to target the emissions at their sources."  For my next run I think I'll stick to my local park.  * Melissa Hogenboom is a senior health correspondent at the BBC and author of Breadwinners and The Motherhood Complex. She is melissa_hogenboom on Instagram.  ** All content within this article is provided for general information only, and should not be treated as a substitute for the medical advice of health care professionals. -- For trusted insights on health and wellbeing, sign up to the Health Fix newsletter by senior health correspondent Melissa Hogenboom who also writes the Live Well For Longer and Six Steps to Calm courses.   For more science, technology, environment and health stories from the BBC, follow us on Facebook   and Instagram . ##段落
19小时前 分享 保存 在Google上添加为首选 梅丽莎·霍根布姆 总体而言，运动的好处大于空气污染带来的风险。但我们可以采取一些措施来尽量减少暴露。最近一次晨跑时，我在路口等红灯，一辆货车停在我旁边。我忍不住吸了一大口浓重的尾气。作为一名住在伦敦的热衷骑行和跑步的人，这几乎无法避免。主动出行已融入我的日常通勤，所以我经常在等红灯时被困在车流后面。每当我咳出最新一波污染的空气时，我常常想：在污染的道路上锻炼，对我而言弊大于利吗？以下是你需要了解的关于风险与益处的一切，以及在城市环境中锻炼时如何最好地保护自己。

##段落
你呼吸的空气里有什么？众所周知，空气污染与多种慢性健康问题相关，包括心脏病、呼吸系统疾病、癌症以及更高的早逝风险。据世界卫生组织统计，全球99%的人口呼吸着受污染的空气，每年导致670万人过早死亡。伦敦帝国理工学院副教授、研究污染对运动影响的奥黛丽·德·纳泽尔说，空气污染几乎影响你身体的所有器官。"我们过去认为它只导致呼吸系统疾病，但它也与心血管疾病、糖尿病、认知功能和生殖影响有关，"她说。一个主要担忧是PM2.5，即直径仅为2.5微米的微小颗粒。这些细微颗粒大约比人类头发丝的宽度小30倍。它们从交通中直接释放到空气中，能够深入我们的肺部，进入血液并在全身循环。随着时间的推移，这种颗粒积累会影响大脑。在2025年一项涵盖51项研究的综述中，一个团队分析了超过2900万人的数据，发现三种空气污染与帕金森病风险增加之间存在关联。其中之一就是PM2.5。"当颗粒这么小时，它们可以穿过血脑屏障，对血管和屏障造成损害，但最终也会进入你的大脑，"该研究的合著者、剑桥大学流行病学家哈宁·赫里斯说。但还有其他污染物。在繁忙道路旁或城市中锻炼时，我们会吸入二氧化氮，该综述也发现它会增加帕金森病的风险。二氧化氮还被认为会导致肺部炎症。从长远来看，它会损害我们肺部的发育和功能。此外还有二氧化硫、氨、一氧化碳，甚至地面臭氧。

##段落
当我们跑步、骑车或剧烈运动时，呼吸会变得更快更深。这意味着与步行相比，跑步时我们往往会吸入更多受污染的空气。在覆盖相同距离的情况下，高强度运动会让人吸入更大剂量的有毒颗粒进入肺部。但也许出乎意料的是，坐在车里并不能完全让你免受空气污染的影响。“骑车时的个人暴露量实际上比坐在车里更低，”伦敦帝国理工学院NHS信托基金的呼吸科顾问医师兼肺癌专家鲁迪·辛哈拉伊说。“而当你骑车时，你往往会移动得更多一些。空气流动也更大一些。”而且不仅仅是交通污染，伦敦和纽约等城市的地铁交通中也可能含有高浓度的细颗粒物，其中很多是车轮、轨道和刹车摩擦产生的富含金属的粉尘。“好消息是，在污染城市中锻炼所带来的益处大于风险，”德纳泽尔说。事实上，她说，运动本身可能正在保护我们的身体免受污染侵害。在2016年的一项研究中，德纳泽尔和同事正是对此进行了探究。在一项建模研究中，他们估计步行和骑车的健康收益超过了脏空气带来的危害。只有在污染水平异常高的情况下，比如印度德里等世界上一些污染最严重的城市，风险才开始接近或超过长时间锻炼的益处。而且即使在污染地区，运动也能降低早逝风险。最近的一篇综述论文发现，与不运动相比，在空气污染环境中锻炼与死亡风险降低26%相关。可以预料的是，在更清洁的空气中锻炼被发现更为可取，并且风险降低幅度更高，达到31%。德纳泽尔说，对于生活在城市环境中的人来说，这应该令人鼓舞。然而，户外锻炼的益处并不一定总能超过空气污染的风险——考虑自身的健康状况很重要。那些已有健康问题的人，比如哮喘或心血管疾病患者，应该更加谨慎。其他研究发现，在污染地区，运动仍能改善肺功能并降低血压。它还可以抵消污染对认知的一些影响。然而，你呼吸的空气有多污染也会产生很大差别。2018年，辛哈拉伊和同事招募了健康志愿者以及患有慢性阻塞性肺病或冠心病的老年人参与研究。参与者被要求要么在公园里，要么沿着伦敦一条繁忙街道步行两小时。研究团队发现，仅仅两次

##段落
数小时后，在空气更清洁区域步行者的肺功能和血管功能有所改善。而在高污染区域步行者的获益则较小。对于慢阻肺患者，污染暴露与症状加重相关。换句话说，运动可以抵消污染的许多危害，但反过来也一样：重度污染会削弱运动带来的保护效应，甚至还会削弱运动对认知的益处。因此，大多数情况下运动的益处大于风险，但在污染空气中运动仍然不理想。

##段落
对于我们这些生活在大城市的人来说，不可能干脆搬到乡下去慢跑。但次优选择是找到附近最绿、最不拥堵的区域。比如，我早上通勤时可以选择沿一条车流较少的道路骑行，但确实会多花几分钟。de Nazelle 表示，研究表明，远离交通繁忙路段一两条街，就能将污染暴露减少20%到30%。如果你能走小路，那就更好了。一项研究发现，选择小路而非繁忙路线可将暴露减少50%。

##段落

• 每天运动五分钟可能帮助数百万人更长寿
• 举重如何帮助你在衰老过程中保持更健康

##段落
如果可能的话，避开高峰时段也是个好主意。Khreis 说，汽车在拥堵中怠速不动会形成“污染热点”。她建议，同样要留意炎热晴朗午后的臭氧峰值。她解释说，这种强效化学物质往往在非常炎热且阳光充足时形成。把这些因素与高峰时段的空气污染叠加在一起，会进一步加剧问题。

##段落
最后，监测当地空气质量污染指数可能会有帮助。这些指数可以告诉你所在区域在任何一天的水平。Sinharay 建议，在空气污染较重的日子，室内或公园运动是更好的选择。

##段落
不过，Khreis 表示，从更大层面来看，政策改变将产生比我们个人层面所做努力更有意义的影响。“这很大程度上是一个系统性问题。虽然那些个人选择可以帮助我们减少自身暴露，但最有效的防护仍然是从源头治理排放。”

##段落
至于我下一次跑步，我想我还是会坚持去附近的公园。

readings.title: 6 ways to give that aren’t about money
body: Good news: You can be a generous person without writing a bunch of checks. In fact, many of the most awe-inspiring and effective examples of generosity are gifts of time and energy, talent and love, custom-fitted to a specific need. This type of giving is open to everyone.
Many of the most awe-inspiring and effective examples of generosity are gifts of time and energy, talent and love, custom-fitted to a specific need.

Not sure where to begin? Here are six gifts of time and attention that have the strong potential to spark ripple effects that affect millions, from head of TED Chris Anderson’s new book, Infectious Generosity .

Zen master Thich Nhat Hanh taught that attention is the most precious gift we can give someone. This is where generosity starts — with a willingness to stop focusing on ourselves and to instead pay attention to someone else and their needs. From that act of connection, anything can happen.

Truth is, it can be difficult. We spend much of our time lost in our own worlds. We are often reluctant to focus on the issues that others are dealing with. So we put up shields. And that means that many of the people who could really use our attention never feel seen by us. The generosity of attention is therefore the generosity of being willing to be a little uncomfortable, to take down those shields, to give up some time, to risk coming to care about someone else.
Whether you stop and have a meaningful connection with a person in need or spend 30 minutes researching a cause you think might matter, you have already begun your generosity journey.

In our connected era, there’s a type of generosity that matters more than ever: a willingness to reach out to those with whom we disagree with. Many disputes today play out in public online. Huge audiences can become glued to online feuds. What if we could bring a satisfying resolution to more of these conflicts?

It’s hard to reach out to our critics. This is a particularly challenging form of the generosity mindset. You are sacrificing your personal comfort for the greater good of bringing people together. But if you’re successful, there’s a powerful knock-on benefit: You are helping change the tone of public discussion today. That’s a gift to all of us.
The single greatest gift we can give is knowledge — knowledge that solves a problem, fills a need or opens a pathway forward.
In countless circumstances, the single greatest gift we can give is knowledge — knowledge that solves a problem, fills a need or opens a pathway forward.

Our single biggest piece of advice to someone coming to speak on the TED stage is to think of their talk not as an opportunity to pitch something (like a business or a cause) but rather as a gift. It is a chance to freely share valuable ideas with the audience. And those ideas have the potential to impact a listener’s life for years to come.

If you possess knowledge that others may benefit from, consider how you could share it to create ripple effects. What may take you a few hours to prepare and act on could light up someone’s life — and that could just be the beginning.

In our connected age, the networks we have access to matter more than ever. Therefore, one of the most important forms of viral generosity is to help people connect with others. The simplest way to do this is to make an introduction.

As psychologist and TED speaker Adam Grant has argued, an introduction can be fairly easy to give — and unbelievably valuable to receive. Ask many people how they met their partner, got their dream job or found the perfect collaborator for their creative project, and the answer will often be the same: someone — a friend, a neighbor, a colleague — introduced them to the right person. What you’re effectively doing is giving someone else access to your network of resources. And those introductions can have exponential consequences.

In his remarkable book Human Universals , anthropologist Donald Brown documented how hospitality is one of hundreds of human behaviors that have been observed in every single culture ever studied. But if hospitality is so ubiquitous (and so pleasant), is it really a form of generosity? Well, yes. Quite apart from any costs involved, it takes effort to invite someone over, whether friends or possible future friends. It’s easier just to watch the next episode of the TV series you’re into.
So how can hospitality contribute to infectious generosity? Hospitality taps into our deepest instincts for connection to one another. And each experience of it evokes a desire to reciprocate.
People need money, food, shelter and healthcare, to be sure. But we also yearn for beauty, wonder, laughter, transcendence — all elements of enchantment.

Pioneering artist Lily Yeh was approached by the dancer and choreographer Arthur L. Hall to undertake a community art project in a derelict, abandoned plot in her home city of Philadelphia. “I was interested but totally scared,” Yeh recalled. “I had little resources and no experience in working outdoors in a community setting. I wanted to run away, but I did not want to see a coward in the mirror. So I stepped into the project.”

The community project became the Village of Arts and Humanities, an art park full of trees, sculptures and mosaics created by local adults and children in collaboration with Yeh. Yeh’s work led her to a profound realization: that creating beauty in public spaces is profoundly healing and transformative for communities.

People need money, food, shelter and healthcare, to be sure. But we also yearn for beauty, wonder, laughter, transcendence — all elements of enchantment. Those who can enchant can offer a gift of immense value.

好消息是：你不必开出一堆支票也能成为一个慷慨的人。事实上，许多最令人惊叹、最有效的慷慨之举，是时间与精力、才华与爱的馈赠，是为特定需求量身定制的。这种付出对每个人都敞开大门。
##段落
许多最令人惊叹、最有效的慷慨之举，是时间与精力、才华与爱的馈赠，是为特定需求量身定制的。
##段落
不知从何开始？以下是六种时间与关注的馈赠，它们极有可能引发波及数百万人的涟漪效应，出自TED负责人克里斯·安德森的新书《传染性慷慨》。
##段落
1. 转移注意力
禅宗大师一行禅师曾教导说，注意力是我们能给予他人最珍贵的礼物。慷慨正是从这里开始——愿意停止关注自己，转而关注他人及其需求。从这种联结的行为出发，一切皆有可能。
##段落
事实是，这并不容易。我们大部分时间都沉浸在自己的世界里。我们常常不愿去关注他人正在面对的问题。于是我们竖起盾牌。这意味着，许多真正需要我们关注的人，从未感到被我们看见。因此，注意力的慷慨，就是愿意让自己稍微不舒服、放下那些盾牌、付出一些时间、冒险去关心他人的慷慨。
##段落
无论你是停下来与一个需要帮助的人建立有意义的联结，还是花30分钟研究一个你认为可能重要的议题，你都已经踏上了自己的慷慨之旅。
##段落
2. 搭建桥梁
在我们这个互联的时代，有一种慷慨比以往任何时候都更重要：愿意主动接触那些与我们意见相左的人。如今许多争端都在公开的网络上上演。庞大的受众会紧盯网络骂战。如果我们能为更多这类冲突带来令人满意的化解，那会怎样？
##段落
主动接触批评我们的人并不容易。这是一种尤其具有挑战性的慷慨心态。你是在牺牲个人的舒适，以换取将人们团结在一起的更大善果。但如果你成功了，就会产生强大的连锁效应：你在帮助改变当今公共讨论的基调。那是给我们所有人的礼物。
##段落
我们能给予的唯一最伟大的礼物就是知识——解决问题的知识、满足需求的知识，或开辟前路的知识。
##段落
3. 分享知识
在无数情况下，我们能给予的唯一最伟大的礼物就是知识——解决问题的知识、满足需求的知识，或开辟前路的知识。
##段落
我们给某人的唯一最重要的建议

##段落
在TED舞台上演讲，意味着演讲者不应把自己的演讲视为推销某样东西（比如一项业务或一项事业）的机会，而应把它当作一份礼物。这是一个自由地与观众分享宝贵想法的机会。而这些想法有可能在未来数年里持续影响听众的人生。
##段落
如果你拥有能让他人受益的知识，不妨想想如何将它分享出去，以产生涟漪效应。你花几个小时准备和付诸行动的事情，可能点亮某个人的人生——而这或许仅仅是开始。
##段落
4. 促成连接
在我们这个互联的时代，我们所能触及的人脉网络比以往任何时候都更加重要。因此，最具影响力的“病毒式慷慨”形式之一，就是帮助人们与他人建立连接。最简单的方式就是做一次引荐。
##段落
正如心理学家、TED演讲者亚当·格兰特所言，引荐这件事给出时相当容易——而收到时却价值不可估量。问问许多人他们是如何遇到伴侣、获得梦想工作，或为创意项目找到完美合作者的，答案往往如出一辙：某个人——一位朋友、邻居、同事——把他们介绍给了对的人。你实际上做的，是让别人得以接入你的人脉资源网络。而这些引荐可能产生指数级的连锁效应。
##段落
5. 给予款待
人类学家唐纳德·布朗在其杰出著作《人类共性》中记录道，款待是所有被研究过的文化中都能观察到的数百种人类行为之一。但如果款待如此普遍（又如此令人愉悦），它真的算是一种慷慨吗？答案是肯定的。撇开其中涉及的各种成本不谈，邀请某人来家里做客——无论是朋友还是可能成为朋友的人——本身就需要付出心力。相比之下，直接看下一集你追的剧要轻松得多。
##段落
那么，款待如何能推动“传染式慷慨”？款待触及了我们内心深处对彼此连接的渴望。而每一次被款待的体验，都会唤起一种想要回报的愿望。
##段落
人们固然需要金钱、食物、住所和医疗保健。但我们也渴望美、惊奇、欢笑、超越——这些都是“迷人体验”的要素。
##段落
6. 创造迷人体验
先锋艺术家莉莉·叶曾受邀于舞蹈家兼编舞家亚瑟·L·霍尔，在她家乡费城一块荒废破败的地块上开展一个社区艺术项目。“我很感兴趣，但完全被吓到了，”叶回忆道，“我资源匮乏，也没有在社区环境中户外工作的经验。我想逃跑，但我不想在镜子里看到一个懦夫。于是我迈步走进了这个项目。”
##段落
这个社区项目后来成为了“艺术与人文村”——一座充满树木、雕塑和马赛克的艺术公园，全部由当地居民共同创造。

## 与Yeh合作，为儿童和老年人提供服务。Yeh的工作让她深刻认识到：在公共空间创造美，对社区具有深远的疗愈和变革力量。

## 人们需要金钱、食物、住所和医疗保健，这是毫无疑问的。但我们也渴望美、惊奇、欢笑、超越——这些都是魅力的元素。那些能够施展魅力的人，能够赠予他人一份无价的礼物。

## 摘自克里斯·安德森的《传染性慷慨》，经皇冠出版集团授权。版权所有 © 2024 克里斯·安德森。保留所有权利。未经出版商书面许可，不得复制或转载本摘录的任何部分。

## 关于作者：克里斯·安德森是TED的策展人。

## 书籍摘录 克里斯·安德森 慷慨 如何成为更好的人 传染性慷慨 我们人类

readings.title: Why are more Americans moving to Ireland?
body: 15 April 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Anne Cassidy In a historic reversal, the number of Americans moving to Ireland last year was higher than the number of Irish people migrating to the US. Was this just a blip or the start of a more profound trend? Michael Sable is an American stand-up comedian and communications manager who moved from Washington DC to Dublin in 2016.  Sable, who draws on his experience of being an American living in the Republic of Ireland in his stand-up routine, says that, when he first arrived, many Irish people he met were surprised he'd made the move, but now they don't question it.  "I've noticed that, as the years go on, people have been less and less incredulous when hearing that an American moved to Ireland," he says.  Sable is one of a rising number of people who have moved to Ireland from the US, with the latest data showing the figure nearly doubling from  4,900 to 9,600 between 2024 and 2025 ,  exceeding the number of Irish people headed in the opposite direction.   It comes as the US saw more people leave than arrive last year, according to a report from US think tank the  Brookings Institution . It said this was the first time that this had been the case "in at least half a century".  The think tank highlighted "dramatic changes in immigration policy" under the second administration of President Trump, including more removals of undocumented foreign workers, and the White House "all but suspend[ing]" the US programme for accepting refugees.    Separately, more American citizens are choosing to move abroad than ever before, says the  Wall Street Journal.  It calculated that "at least 180,000 Americans" voluntarily left the US in 2025, which it said was a record high.   The reversal in the flow of migration between Ireland and the US marks a historic turning point in the shared history of the two countries, which have deep-rooted ties.  For centuries, millions of Irish people emigrated to the US in search of work or a better life, making Irish Americans one of the country's largest ethnic groups. There have been several US presidents with Irish ancestry, including John F Kennedy and Joe Biden, whose visits to Ireland were  celebrated more like homecomings  than diplomatic missions.   Irish writer Colm Tóibín has frequently explored the relationship between Ireland and the US in his work, particularly in his novels, Brooklyn and Long Island, which follow the story of an Irish girl who emigrates to America in the 1950s.  Tóibín, who lives in the US, says the relationship between the US and Ireland has changed. "A myth was created that America was a great place of opportunity and wealth," he says. "It was built into the [Irish] culture that if there's any trouble, you go to England, if there's any ambition or spark you go to America." "The flow of young people [from Ireland to the US] looking for work just hasn't continued. So, that is going to be a big change in the future, because you're not going to get the same easy connection between Ireland and America," he adds.  The trend partly reflects political shifts in both countries. As well as developing into a high-tech, export-driven knowledge economy, Ireland has undergone a social transformation in recent decades, moving from a deeply conservative society to a liberal, progressive nation, following referendums on divorce, abortion and gay marriage.    Tóibín, who was a prominent campaigner for the "yes" vote in Ireland’s same-sex marriage referendum, says: "Everyone became more aware that Ireland was a more liberal, cosmopolitan, open society, and that it would be a good place to live." By contrast, the US has moved to the political right under President Trump, who, since returning to office, has launched a major crackdown on illegal immigration.   Tóibín revisits the Irish-American immigrant experience in his latest short story collection, The News from Dublin. In one story in the collection, Five Bridges, the protagonist is an undocumented Irish immigrant preparing to leave America before US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, known as Ice, come looking for him. The number of Irish citizens deported from the US  rose by more than 50%  in 2025.  "There are large numbers of Irish people in America who are official in every way – they pay taxes, own their own house, have kids in school, but they came in on a tourist visa," says Tóibín. "If Ice found them, Ice would detain them. That's really frightening." Expatsi, a firm that helps US citizens to move abroad,  reported it experienced a month's worth of traffic  in the hours after President Trump's election in 2024. Expatsi co-founder Jen Barnett says the reasons Americans cite for leaving are wide-ranging. "[Factors include] what's going on politically in the US, and has been for 10 years, the cost of living, and then safety. Gun violence is so prevalent," she says.  Politics was also a driving factor for Kevin Wozniak, an American lecturer living in Ireland. He and his husband left Boston in 2023 after he got a post at Maynooth University, 23km (14 miles) west of Dublin.  "My motivation to look at opportunities abroad was deep fears about the trajectory of the country in the era of Donald Trump," Wozniak says. "Ireland has liberalised very significantly and has moved in exactly the opposite direction that the US is moving." Natalia Lange, a migrant support worker based in Crosshaven, county Cork, moved there from Michigan with her husband after the 2024 US election. Lange, who is half-Hungarian and has an EU passport, dreamed of living in Ireland since visiting on a school trip. "Politically, Ireland aligns much more with how we think," she says. "The US has the infrastructure to take in a lot more people, but it's a lot less inviting." Lauren Udoh, from Houston, Texas, moved to Claregalway, in county Galway, in 2021 after marrying her Irish husband. Udoh, who has two young children, works as an executive assistant and documents expat life on social media under the moniker TheGalwayGal.  "One of the biggest benefits is safety. I feel a lot safer here," she says. "With kids going to school, you don’t have to worry about school shootings." Emigration from Ireland has fallen, with 65,600 people leaving in the year to April 2025, a  6% decrease on 2024 , according to the Irish Central Statistics Office (CSO). For those wanting to live abroad, Australia is the most popular destination.  The CSO said 13,500 people left Ireland for Australia in the year to April 2025, the highest level since 2013. This is more than double the estimated 6,100 people who left Ireland for the US, which was, however, still up 22% on the previous year.   Restrictions around J1 visas, which allow Irish university students to work and travel in the US, has caused many  Irish students to rethink studying in the US.    Karen McHugh, CEO at Safe Home Ireland, an organisation supporting Irish-born emigrants wishing to return to Ireland, says: "We've certainly noticed an increase in queries about returning [from the US to Ireland]," she says. "Australia and Canada are two major countries where people are now going to from Ireland, and that's ease of getting a visa." Irish student Jamie McElhinney is currently on a work placement in Portugal as part of his hospitality management course. McElhinney, who studies at Dundalk Institute of Technology, says current immigration controls put him off seeking a work placement in the US. "I was going to go to Boston, and then all of the news about Ice started coming out. It’s a deterrent from going over there," he says.  While there are opportunities in Ireland, with  employment at 74.4%,  there is also a growing housing crisis, with recent  protests  over the shortage of affordable housing.  Barnett says the housing shortage is something the Americans her company helps to relocate are mindful of, adding: "They don't want to add to [the housing crisis], so one of the things we talk to them about is staying out of city centres." Sable, whose Irish grandparents emigrated to the US in 1939, is one of many Americans whose ancestry enabled them to get an Irish passport. Applications for Irish passports in the US rose by 10% in 2024 , the Irish Department of Foreign Affairs reported.  Sable now thinks of Ireland as home. "Culturally, I identify a lot more with Irish people," he says. "It's a very collective society, not huge on individualism like in the US." More like this:  •  Why Ireland's film industry is booming    •  Is New York's cannabis business flying high?   •  The 'brutal' toll of war on Dubai’s tourist trade Bill Hillyard, another American with Irish roots, relocated to Ireland for the cooler climate. He and his wife Anne left California following wildfires in 2019. "My wife said we need to move somewhere where it rains." They now run a pub called The Algiers in Baltimore, Co Cork.  Hillyard says he now tries to avoid turbulent events in the US. "I tried not to follow the news because I'm here now," he says. "But I'm reminded every day, because everyone asks me about Trump and what's going on there… I'm West Cork's ambassador to the US at this point." -- For global insights and expert analysis for the boardroom and beyond, sign up to the  World of Business newsletter , while  The Essential List  delivers a handpicked selection of features and insights. For more on business and beyond, follow us on  LinkedIn . Business Migration Features World of Business

##段落
2026年4月15日 分享 收藏 在Google中添加为首选 Anne Cassidy

##段落
去年，移居爱尔兰的美国人数量超过了移居美国的爱尔兰人，这是一次历史性的逆转。这只是一时的反常，还是一个更深刻趋势的开端？

##段落
迈克尔·塞布尔是一位美国单口喜剧演员兼传播经理，2016年从华盛顿特区搬到了都柏林。塞布尔将自己在爱尔兰共和国生活的美国人经历融入脱口秀表演中。他说，刚到这里时，许多他遇到的爱尔兰人对他做出这一选择感到惊讶，但现在他们不再质疑了。“我注意到，随着时间推移，人们听到美国人移居爱尔兰时，越来越不觉得不可思议了，”他说。

##段落
塞布尔是从美国移居爱尔兰的人数不断增长中的一员。最新数据显示，这一数字在2024年至2025年间几乎翻倍，从4900人增至9600人，超过了反向移居美国的爱尔兰人数量。

##段落
与此同时，根据美国智库布鲁金斯学会的一份报告，去年离开美国的人数超过了入境人数。报告称，这是“至少半个世纪以来”首次出现这种情况。该智库重点指出了特朗普第二任期内“移民政策的剧烈变化”，包括加大遣返无证外籍工人的力度，以及白宫“几乎暂停”了美国接收难民的项目。

##段落
另据《华尔街日报》报道，选择移居海外的美国公民人数比以往任何时候都多。该报测算，2025年“至少有18万美国人”自愿离开美国，称这是历史最高纪录。

##段落
爱尔兰与美国之间移民流向的逆转，标志着两国共同历史中的一个历史性转折点。两国有着根深蒂固的联系。几个世纪以来，数百万爱尔兰人移民美国，寻求工作或更好的生活，使爱尔兰裔美国人成为美国最大的族裔群体之一。多位美国总统拥有爱尔兰血统，包括约翰·F·肯尼迪和乔·拜登，他们对爱尔兰的访问更像是荣归故里，而非外交使命。

##段落
爱尔兰作家科尔姆·托宾在其作品中频繁探讨爱尔兰与美国的关系，尤其是在他的小说《布鲁克林》和《长岛》中，讲述了一位1950年代移民美国的爱尔兰女孩的故事。现居美国的托宾表示，美国与爱尔兰之间的关系已经改变。“人们创造了一个神话，说美国是一个充满机遇和财富的好地方，”他说。“这已经融入了（爱尔兰）文化——如果有麻烦，你去英国；如果有抱负……

## "否则你就去美国。"他补充道："年轻人（从爱尔兰前往美国）寻找工作的潮流并没有延续下去。因此，这将是未来的一个重大变化，因为爱尔兰与美国之间那种轻松便捷的联系将不复存在。"

## 这一趋势部分反映了两国的政治变迁。爱尔兰不仅发展成为一个高科技、出口导向型知识经济体，近几十年来还经历了深刻的社会转型——在离婚、堕胎和同性婚姻公投之后，从一个极度保守的社会转变为一个自由、进步的国家。

## 托宾曾是爱尔兰同性婚姻公投中"赞成"阵营的知名活动人士，他说："每个人都越来越意识到，爱尔兰是一个更自由、更具世界主义精神、更开放的社会，是一个宜居之地。"相比之下，美国在特朗普总统领导下转向政治右翼，特朗普自重返白宫以来，已对非法移民展开了大规模打击。

## 托宾在其最新短篇小说集《都柏林消息》中重新审视了爱尔兰裔美国移民的经历。其中一篇小说《五座桥》的主人公是一名无证爱尔兰移民，他正准备在美国移民和海关执法局（简称ICE）找上门之前离开美国。2025年，被美国驱逐出境的爱尔兰公民人数上升了50%以上。

## "在美国有大量爱尔兰人在各方面都是合法的——他们纳税、拥有自己的房子、孩子在上学，但他们是持旅游签证入境的，"托宾说，"如果ICE找到他们，ICE就会拘留他们。这真的很可怕。"

## Expatsi是一家帮助美国公民移居海外的公司，据其报告，2024年特朗普当选总统后的数小时内，其网站流量就达到了平时一个月的水平。Expatsi联合创始人珍·巴内特表示，美国人给出的离开理由多种多样。她说："（因素包括）美国政治上正在发生的事情，而且已经持续了10年，还有生活成本，然后是安全问题。枪支暴力太普遍了。"

## 政治也是居住在爱尔兰的美国讲师凯文·沃兹尼亚克的驱动力。2023年，他在都柏林以西23公里（14英里）的梅努斯大学获得了一个职位后，和丈夫一起离开了波士顿。

## "我寻找海外机会的动机，是对唐纳德·特朗普时代这个国家发展轨迹的深切担忧，"沃兹尼亚克说，"爱尔兰已经非常显著地走向自由化，其方向与美国正在走的方向恰恰相反。"

## 娜塔莉亚·兰格是科克郡克罗斯黑文的一名移民支持工作者，她在2024年美国大选后与丈夫从密歇根州搬到了那里。兰格有一半匈牙利血统，持有欧盟护照，她梦想在爱尔兰生活。

##段落
她曾参加学校组织的旅行到访过这里。“在政治层面，爱尔兰与我们的想法契合得多，”她说，“美国有接纳更多人的基础设施，但对外来者远没有那么友好。”来自得克萨斯州休斯敦的劳伦·乌多，在嫁给爱尔兰丈夫后，于2021年搬到了戈尔韦郡的克莱尔戈尔韦。乌多有两个年幼的孩子，从事行政助理工作，并以TheGalwayGal的网名在社交媒体上记录外籍生活。“最大的好处之一是安全。我在这里感觉安全多了，”她说，“孩子上学，你不用担心中学校枪击。”根据爱尔兰中央统计局的数据，爱尔兰的移出人口有所下降，截至2025年4月的一年里有65600人离开，较2024年减少6%。对于想移居国外的人来说，澳大利亚是最受欢迎的目的地。爱尔兰中央统计局称，截至2025年4月的一年里有13500人离开爱尔兰前往澳大利亚，为2013年以来的最高水平。这比估计前往美国的6100人多出一倍以上，不过后者仍比上年增长22%。J1签证允许爱尔兰大学生在美国工作和旅行，但相关限制已导致许多爱尔兰学生重新考虑赴美学习。Safe Home Ireland是一家为希望返回爱尔兰的爱尔兰裔移居者提供支持的组织，其首席执行官凯伦·麦休说：“我们确实注意到，关于（从美国返回爱尔兰）的咨询有所增加。”她说：“澳大利亚和加拿大是爱尔兰人现在前往的两个主要国家，因为签证容易拿到。”爱尔兰学生杰米·麦克尔希尼目前正在葡萄牙进行工作实习，这是他酒店管理课程的一部分。就读于邓多克理工学院的麦克尔希尼说，当前的移民管制让他不愿去美国实习。“我本来要去波士顿，后来所有关于Ice的消息开始传出来。这让人不敢去那边，”他说。虽然爱尔兰也有机会，就业率为74.4%，但住房危机也在加剧，近期还因可负担住房短缺而爆发抗议。巴尼特说，她公司协助搬迁的美国人会留意住房短缺问题，并补充说：“他们不想给（住房危机）雪上加霜，所以我们和他们谈的一件事就是不要住在市中心。”萨布尔的祖父母于1939年从爱尔兰移居美国，他是众多因血统而获得爱尔兰护照的美国人之一。爱尔兰外交部报告称，2024年在美国的爱尔兰护照申请量上升了10%。萨布尔现在把爱尔兰视为家。“在文化上，我更认同爱尔兰人，”他说，“这是一个非常……”

##在美国，个人主义盛行，而这里更偏向集体社会。类似内容：• 爱尔兰电影产业为何蓬勃发展 • 纽约的大麻生意是否蒸蒸日上？ • 战争对迪拜旅游业的“残酷”冲击

##另一位有爱尔兰血统的美国人比尔·希利亚德，为了更凉爽的气候搬到了爱尔兰。2019年野火之后，他和妻子安妮离开了加利福尼亚。“我妻子说，我们得搬到一个会下雨的地方。”他们现在在科克郡巴尔的摩经营一家名为“阿尔及尔”的酒吧。希利亚德说，他现在尽量避开美国的动荡新闻。“我尽量不看新闻，因为我现在在这里，”他说，“但我每天都会被提醒，因为每个人都在问我特朗普的事，还有那边发生了什么……我现在简直是西科克驻美国大使。”

readings.title: The AI threat keeping scientists up at night
body: Technology The AI threat keeping scientists up at night ﻿Claude, design a doomsday bioweapon. Make no mistakes. by Eric Levitz Sep 19, 2026, 10:00 AM UTC Gift Getty Images Eric Levitz is a senior correspondent at Vox. He covers a wide range of political and policy issues with a special focus on questions that internally divide the American left and right. Before coming to Vox in 2024, he wrote a column on politics and economics for New York Magazine. AI will be the death of me. And you. And everyone we know. At least, this is what a growing number of technologists and policymakers fear. Last week, a lead researcher at Anthropic declared that there was a greater than 10 percent chance of AI “killing all humans” within the next decade. This nerve-racking forecast, combined with recent AI-initiated cyberattacks , have fueled calls for slowing the progress of artificial intelligence — a proposal that Anthropic and OpenAI subsequently embraced. Not all prophets of AI doom agree about precisely how this apocalypse would come about. Many focus on scenarios reminiscent of The Terminator films, in which superintelligent machines conspire to exterminate humanity — perhaps in the same not-quite-intentional way that humans laid waste to the dodo, or passenger pigeon. Synthetic pandemics are among the biggest existential risks facing humanity. AI could make bioweapons more powerful and easier to build. Governments can make us safer from both natural and artificial pathogens by investing more into pandemic preparedness. But there is another, arguably more intuitive way that AI could bring about mass death, if not human extinction: by making it easier for people to develop and deploy catastrophic bioweapons. Importantly, this hypothetical doesn’t require AI models to become conscious or superintelligent; it merely requires them to accelerate preexisting trends in biotechnology. For those alarmed by this hypothetical, the threat AI poses is essentially twofold. First, when combined with technological progress in gene editing and DNA synthesis, chatbots could vastly increase the number of people capable of assembling dangerous viruses already known to medical science. And the more potential bioengineers there are in the world, the higher the odds that one will prove to be a diligent psychopath. Second, AI could help highly trained biologists to discover — or engineer — a custom supervirus, which could then fall into the wrong hands. Recent headlines have lent some credence to both of these fears. Earlier this year, biologists warned that, with a few simple prompts, they’d gotten chatbots to dispense detailed instructions for engineering a treatment-resistant strain of an infamous pathogen, step-by-step protocols for recreating a once-pandemic virus, and advice on dispersing biological payloads via weather balloon. In August, a team of scientists revealed that an AI model trained on DNA sequences had generated blueprints for deadly viruses unseen in nature (albeit, viruses deadly to bacteria , not animals). And last week, Anthropic announced that it had thwarted several suspected attempts by state actors to use Claude for bioweapons research. Precisely how much AI is increasing the risk of an artificial pandemic is unclear. Even before ChatGPT, advances in synthetic biology were already making bioengineering tools more potent and accessible. And even after four years of rapid AI progress, the technical barriers to engineering novel superviruses remain formidable. Regardless, there is a great deal more that governments can — and should — be doing to protect us from synthetic pandemics, both manmade and natural. No matter what AI’s ultimate impact on biosecurity proves to be, now is the time to both prepare for the worst-case scenario and, ideally, preempt it. Before we dig into how AI could raise the risk of a man-made pandemic, it’s worth spelling out why that prospect is so unnerving. Put simply, few things could more credibly destroy civilization — and/or, the human species — than a synthetic supervirus. Infectious diseases have killed more humans than any other force on Earth. The Black Death wiped out at least 30 percent of all Europeans in the 1300s , while the 1918 flu killed 50 million people worldwide. You don’t need me to tell you what things were like in 2020 (or how much worse they could have been, if vaccines hadn’t been rolled out in record time). And nature kicked off these catastrophes without even trying. A bioterrorist consciously seeking to maximize human death could theoretically improve on evolution’s handiwork. If biotech continues to advance — and scientists identify viral genomes that reliably yield high transmissibility and lethality — a malicious actor might one day be able to manufacture a virus that’s both as contagious as measles and as deadly as Ebola. Natural selection generally disfavors viruses that are both highly transmissible and profoundly fatal; bugs that kill their hosts too reliably often have difficulty spreading. Yet a virus with a long asymptomatic period could escape this tradeoff. For example, HIV can live in a person’s body for a decade before generating noticeable symptoms. In theory, a highly contagious respiratory virus could similarly lie in wait for many weeks, months, or even years. If bioterrorists ever managed to unleash an easily transmitted, highly fatal virus, they could shake the foundations of modern existence . In that scenario, reliably showing up for work might require accepting a 50-50 chance of getting yourself — and your family — brutally killed. Covid never required essential workers to assume risks anywhere near this high (the virus had a less than 1 percent case fatality rate among prime-age workers, before vaccines became available). Although there are many heroes among us, plenty of doctors, nurses, warehouse workers, power plant technicians, delivery drivers, and other essential laborers might not tolerate a coin flip’s chance of wiping out their loved ones. And if enough sheltered in place, systems for producing and distributing healthcare, food, water, and power could swiftly break down. All this invites the question: Who would ever want to do this? After all, viruses are terrible weapons: They’re difficult to make, impossible to control, and jeopardize the lives of those who cultivate and distribute them. Partly for these reasons, biological weapons have hardly ever been used ; the last fatal bioterror attacks were the anthrax mailings of 2001. To this, anxious biosecurity experts might reply, to quote the former British intelligence officer Alfred Pennyworth : “Some men just want to watch the world burn.” Mass shooters regularly forfeit their lives to the cause of killing others at random. And brilliant iconoclasts periodically develop murderous ideologies; Ted Kaczynski, the Harvard mathematician turned Unabomber, wished to bring about the collapse of industrial civilization. And every once in a while, an aspiring supervillain gets graduate training in virology. In the 1990s, the Kyoto University-educated genetic engineer Seiichi Endo joined Japan’s Aum Shinrikyo death cult. Drawing on the group’s $1 billion in funds , Endo sought to weaponize Ebola , Q fever , botulinum, and anthrax — with the aim of killing as many nonbelievers as possible. Of course, Endo failed. And lone wolf psychopaths have never gotten their hands on anything more lethal than an assault weapon, bomb, or airplane. But some scientists believe that technological advances — including generative AI — may provide the Endos and Kaczynskis of tomorrow with catastrophic power. MIT biologist Kevin Esvelt is among his field’s most prominent Cassandras. And he has voiced two fundamental concerns. The first is that breakthroughs in synthetic biology and AI are rapidly expanding the pool of people who can engineer known viruses. Over the past 15 years, the cost and difficulty of editing genomes have plummeted. In 2012, to modify a specific site in a genome, you often needed access to custom-engineered proteins that cost upward of $5,000 and still tended to work poorly, according to Olivia Scharfman , a biotechnology fellow at the Institute for Progress. Thanks to the gene-editing tool CRISPR , a scientist with minimal lab training can execute such a modification for as little as $30. Meanwhile, DNA synthesis has also grown radically more affordable. This might not be such a big deal, if dangerous biological materials were hard to legally access. But Esvelt and his colleagues recently demonstrated that this isn’t the case . As an experiment, they had a student place orders for pieces of the 1918 influenza genome using a pseudonym and fake position. Thirty-six of 38 DNA synthesis companies shipped the genomes without asking whether the applicant had government permission or sound intentions. Together, these fragments were enough to create the virus many times over. Crucially, in Esvelt’s account, reverse engineering known viruses using modern tools does not require elite skills . Any random biology graduate student may be up to the job. And AI may be making such rudimentary viral engineering even easier. In theory, a chatbot can help you plan a bioweapons attack in much the same way that it can walk you through fixing a dishwasher: By finding and synthesizing the internet’s vast trove of information, offering step-by-step instructions for navigating unfamiliar challenges, and fielding all troubleshooting queries that might subsequently arise. And there’s evidence that AI models will in fact provide would-be bioterrorists with precisely this kind of assistance. In a 2023 study, MIT researchers asked students to seek guidance on engineering a pandemic from that era’s chatbots . Within an hour, the AI models had suggested four promising pathogens, offered detailed protocols for manufacturing them with with synthetic DNA, provided a list of DNA synthesis retailers with low screening standards, and advised that — if users still found themselves unable to make the virus, even with all this help — they could purchase the assistance of a contract research organization to do some of the bioengineering for them. And of course, frontier models have gotten a lot better since 2023. Last year, SecureBio, Esvelt’s biosecurity nonprofit, found that one OpenAI model outperformed 94 percent of expert virologists on troubleshooting complex laboratory problems. Anthropic’s internal research has produced similar results. In one experiment, the company tasked amateurs with drafting a bioweapons acquisition plan . It gave some participants access to basic internet resources and others the assistance of Claude models (with the safeguards turned off). Those working with AI developed far more viable blueprints, according to the biodefense experts who scrutinized the proposals for critical errors. Thus, there’s reason to think that the number of people with the skills and resources necessary for reverse engineering a virus from genomic blueprints is sharply rising — and with it, the risk that a bloodthirsty nihilist or ideologue gets their hands on a dangerous pathogen. What’s even worse than bringing back smallpox? Esvelt’s second concern is that these same technological forces — combined with top scientists’ often reckless ambitions — will lead to the discovery or development of a supervirus, a new or custom-designed pathogen even more dangerous than what nature has come up with in the past. Today, some scientists are actively trying to discover — and publicly identify — novel viruses circulating in nature that could theoretically trigger the next pandemic. Others conduct so-called gain-of-function experiments, altering pathogens to discern which mutations make them more transmissible, lethal, or difficult to detect (some have alleged that Covid-19 emerged from precisely this kind of research , though that theory is widely rejected among epidemiologists ). This work is generally intended to anticipate future epidemiological threats, so that we can develop vaccines before they arrive. But their work could inadvertently provide bad actors with recipes for reverse engineering mass-casualty bioweapons. Separately, advances in gene editing and AI may enable breakthroughs in viral engineering that yield apocalyptic pathogens. A recent study from researchers at Stanford and the Arc Institute fed such fears. The scientists trained an AI called “Evo” on the DNA sequences of bacteriophages, the simple viruses that infect bacteria. They then used this “genomic language model” to generate blueprints for hundreds of bacteriophages found nowhere in nature. Sixteen of these designs yielded viable pathogens, some of which were better at killing bacteria than their natural ancestors. What is clear, however, is that novel pathogens are among the greatest security threats our species faces. Theoretically, scientists may one day be able to engineer novel human viruses using the same basic techniques. What’s more, even if genomic-language models fail at that task, they might still be able to help users tweak existing viruses in ways that render them more transmissible, deadly, or vaccine-resistant. These discoveries could theoretically filter down to amateur bioterrorists or well-funded extremist groups like Aum Shinrikyo. Alternatively, a state-sponsored weapons program could develop a catastrophic supervirus, then unleash it on the world through a lab leak or (perhaps, more improbably) a deliberate attempt at genocide. There is some precedent for the former scenario: The Soviet Union tried to weaponize smallpox and the Marburg virus , despite the considerable hazards and dubious military utility of such bioweapons. In the process, Soviet scientists accidentally triggered a smallpox outbreak during testing, while also letting anthrax leak from a laboratory, killing at least 64 people. All this said, there are reasons to question whether AI is truly making a synthetic pandemic more likely. Chatbots may solve some of the challenges facing an amateur biologist with omnicidal aspirations. But it doesn’t necessarily clear the biggest obstacles in that person’s path. Viral engineering is a complex , difficult, and physical undertaking. Performing it successfully requires what scientists call “ tacit knowledge ” — practical skills and understandings that are difficult to explain in words: knowing how to suppress the hand tremors that could rip delicate DNA strands, or how to recognize when the DNA in your solution has reached the proper concentration, or how to smell when a sample has been contaminated. And these are things that Claude still can’t reliably impart. In studies, amateurs with access to a large language model tend to perform better on written biological challenges — but not on actual lab work. In a 2026 randomized study, non-scientists working with frontier AI systems were no more likely to complete a multistep laboratory assignment than those relying on the internet alone. Of course, tacit knowledge wouldn’t necessarily be a problem for aspiring bioterrorists in the mold of Seiichi Endo — graduate-trained scientists with extensive lab experience. But at a minimum, chatbots don’t appear to have turned every malcontent who once took AP Bio into a competent virologist. And while AI will likely help top biologists advance their field’s frontiers, the barriers to custom engineering doomsday viruses remain formidable. The “Evo” experiment is arguably a case in point. Although the model did generate working blueprints for a few novel bacteriophages, nearly all of its suggested genomes didn’t work. Researchers had to arduously test hundreds of DNA sequences to arrive at 16 viable strands. And engineering slightly modified versions of an extremely small, well-known bacteriophage capable of infecting E. coli in a lab — and creating a novel virus more fearsome than any nature has yet devised — aren’t especially similar tasks. To offer a strained analogy: The fact that I can dunk on Victor Wembanyama in NBA 2K26 does not imply that I’m making progress toward being able to dunk on him in real life. Even in the age of CRISPR and ChatGPT, biology remains an exceptionally difficult discipline that resists reliable modeling . The effects of modifying a single gene can often yield unpredictable and inconsistent results, varying with host biology, immune responses, and environmental conditions that scientists only partly understand. AI may help us overcome these complexities . It also might not. Scientists disagree about how serious a risk synthetic pandemics pose — and how much AI is magnifying it. What is clear, however, is that novel pathogens are among the greatest security threats our species faces. Even if synthetic biology and artificial intelligence did not exist, natural selection would keep churning out new viruses — and periodically hitting upon ones that befuddle human immune systems. For this reason, there would be an urgent need to make our societies less vulnerable to future pandemics, irrespective of AI’s implications for viral engineering. In a world where chatbots and CRISPR are plausibly making bioterrorism easier, failing to invest aggressively in public health is all the more reckless. The good news is we already know — from hard-earned experience — many steps that we can take to reduce the risk of a new pandemic and prepare to respond to one if needed. Governments can limit the destructive power of novel contagions by investing in vaccines that protect against entire families of viruses (or ideally, all of them) and broad-spectrum antivirals ; raise our odds of catching outbreaks early by funding meticulous wastewater and clinical surveillance; ensure that essential workers don’t have to choose between staying alive and keeping civilization going amid a pandemic by developing and then stockpiling foolproof personal protective equipment ; make indoor spaces less hospitable to airborne viruses by upgrading ventilation and filtration systems; and reduce the the threat of bioterrorism by mandating rigorous screening of synthetic-DNA orders . Fears that humanity will be done in by superintelligent machines are currently galvanizing media attention and political concern. And this may be warranted. But we should pay at least as much attention to our species’ age-old, organic adversaries as we do to our hypothetical, robot ones — and not just because the latter could start teaching the former new tricks. ##段落
科技
让科学家夜不能寐的AI威胁
克劳德，设计一件末日生物武器。别出任何差错。
作者：埃里克·莱维茨 2026年9月19日 上午10:00 UTC
赠阅
盖蒂图片社
埃里克·莱维茨是Vox的高级记者。他报道广泛的政治与政策议题，尤其关注在美国左右两派内部造成分歧的问题。在2024年加入Vox之前，他曾为《纽约杂志》撰写政治与经济专栏。

##段落
AI会要了我的命。也会要了你的命。还有我们认识的每一个人。至少，这是越来越多技术专家和政策制定者所担心的。上周，Anthropic的一位首席研究员宣称，未来十年内AI“杀死全人类”的概率超过10%。这一令人神经紧绷的预测，加上近期由AI发起的网络攻击，助推了放缓人工智能发展步伐的呼声——Anthropic和OpenAI随后都对此表示支持。

##段落
并非所有AI末日预言者都对这场灾难将如何具体发生持相同看法。许多人聚焦于类似《终结者》电影的场景：超级智能机器合谋灭绝人类——或许是以一种与人类毁灭渡渡鸟或旅鸽时同样并非完全刻意的方式。

##段落
合成大流行病是人类面临的最大生存风险之一。AI可能使生物武器更强大、更易于制造。政府可以通过加大对大流行病防范的投入，让我们在自然病原体和人造病原体面前都更安全。

##段落
但还有另一种可以说更直观的方式，让AI可能导致大规模死亡——即便不是人类灭绝：那就是让人更容易研发和部署灾难性生物武器。重要的是，这一假设并不要求AI模型变得有意识或具备超级智能；它只要求AI加速生物技术中已有的趋势。

##段落
对于因这一假设而警觉的人来说，AI构成的威胁本质上是双重的。第一，当与基因编辑和DNA合成领域的技术进步相结合时，聊天机器人可能大幅增加有能力组装医学界已知危险病毒的人数。而世界上潜在生物工程师越多，其中出现一个勤勉的精神病态者的概率就越高。第二，AI可能帮助训练有素的生物学家发现——或工程化设计——一种定制超级病毒，而这种病毒随后可能落入不法之手。

##段落
近期的新闻头条为这两种担忧都提供了一定佐证。今年早些时候，生物学家警告说，只需几个简单的提示，他们就让聊天机器人给出了工程化改造一种臭名昭著病原体的耐药毒株的详细说明、重现一种曾经引发大流行的病毒的分步操作流程，以及关于如何分……的建议。

##段落
通过气象气球散播生物载荷。今年8月，一组科学家披露，一个在DNA序列上训练的人工智能模型生成了自然界中不存在的致命病毒的蓝图（尽管这些病毒对细菌致命，而非对动物）。上周，Anthropic宣布，它已挫败了若干由国家行为体涉嫌利用Claude进行生物武器研究的企图。人工智能究竟在多大程度上增加了人为大流行的风险，目前尚不清楚。甚至在ChatGPT出现之前，合成生物学的进步就已经使生物工程工具更加强大、更易于获取。而且即便在人工智能历经四年快速发展之后，工程化新型超级病毒的技术壁垒依然高得惊人。无论如何，各国政府能够——也应当——做更多事情来保护我们免受合成大流行病的威胁，无论是人为的还是自然的。无论人工智能对生物安全的最终影响被证明是什么，现在都是既要为最坏情况做准备、又理想地要抢先阻止它的时候。在我们深入探讨人工智能如何可能提高人为大流行风险之前，值得先阐明为什么这一前景如此令人不安。简而言之，几乎没有比合成超级病毒更能可信地摧毁文明——和/或人类物种——的东西了。传染病杀死的人类比地球上任何其他力量都多。14世纪的黑死病消灭了至少30%的欧洲人，而1918年流感在全球杀死了5000万人。不需要我来告诉你2020年的情况是什么样（也不需要我来告诉你，如果不是疫苗以创纪录的速度推出，情况本可能糟糕多少）。而大自然甚至毫不费力就引发了这些灾难。一个刻意追求最大化人类死亡的生物恐怖分子，理论上可以改进进化的作品。如果生物技术继续进步——并且科学家识别出能够可靠地产生高传播性和高致死率的病毒基因组——那么有朝一日，恶意行为者或许能够制造出一种既像麻疹一样具有传染性、又像埃博拉一样致命的病毒。自然选择通常不利于那些既高度传播又极其致命的病毒；过于可靠地杀死宿主的病原体往往难以传播。然而，一种具有较长无症状期的病毒可以逃脱这种权衡。例如，HIV可以在人体内潜伏十年才产生明显症状。理论上，一种高度传染性的呼吸道病毒同样可以潜伏数周、数月甚至数年。如果生物恐怖分子有朝一日成功释放出一种易于传播、高度致命的病毒，他们可能动摇现代生存的根基。在那种情景下，要可靠地出门上班，可能就需要接受你自己——以及你的家人——有50%的概率被残忍杀害。

##段落
我从未要求任何必要岗位的劳动者去承担接近如此之高的风险（在疫苗问世之前，该病毒在壮年劳动者中的病死率不到1%）。尽管我们中间涌现了许多英雄，但大量医生、护士、仓库工人、电厂技术人员、快递司机以及其他必要劳动者，恐怕未必愿意接受一种如同抛硬币般、可能让至亲丧命的概率。而如果有足够多的人居家避疫，医疗、食品、水和电力的生产与配送体系就可能迅速崩溃。这一切引出一个问题：究竟谁会想干这种事？毕竟，病毒是极其糟糕的武器：制造困难，无法控制，还会危及培育和散布它们的人自身的安全。部分出于这些原因，生物武器几乎从未被真正使用过；最后一次致命的生物恐怖袭击是2001年的炭疽邮件事件。对此，忧心忡忡的生物安全专家或许会引用前英国情报官员阿尔弗雷德·彭尼沃斯的话来回应：“有些人只想看着世界燃烧。”大规模枪击者常常为了随机杀害他人而甘愿付出自己的生命。而才华横溢的反叛者也会周期性地发展出杀人意识形态；从哈佛数学家变为“大学炸弹客”的泰德·卡钦斯基，就希望促成工业文明的崩溃。而每隔一段时间，就会有一个野心勃勃的超级反派接受病毒学的研究生训练。20世纪90年代，京都大学培养的基因工程师远藤诚一加入了日本奥姆真理教这个死亡邪教。借助该组织10亿美元的资金，远藤试图将埃博拉病毒、Q热、肉毒杆菌和炭疽武器化——目标就是尽可能多地杀死异教徒。当然，远藤失败了。而独狼式精神病患者也从未拿到过比突击武器、炸弹或飞机更具杀伤力的东西。但一些科学家认为，包括生成式AI在内的技术进步，可能为未来的远藤们和卡钦斯基们提供灾难性的力量。麻省理工学院生物学家凯文·埃斯维尔特是他所在领域最著名的“卡珊德拉”之一。他表达了两个根本性担忧。第一个担忧是，合成生物学和AI的突破正在迅速扩大能够改造已知病毒的人群范围。过去15年间，编辑基因组的成本和难度大幅下降。根据进步研究所生物技术研究员奥利维亚·沙夫曼的说法，2012年，要想修改基因组中的特定位点，你通常需要获得定制工程蛋白，费用高达5000美元以上，而且往往效果不佳。得益于基因编辑工具CRISPR，一个只受过最少实验室训练的科学家只需30美元就能完成这样的修改。与此同时，DNA合成也在飞速

##段落
便宜得多。如果危险的生物材料在法律上难以获取，这或许算不上什么大事。但埃斯维尔特及其同事最近证明，情况并非如此。作为一项实验，他们让一名学生用假名和虚构职位订购了1918年流感基因组的片段。38家DNA合成公司中有36家在未询问申请人是否获得政府许可或意图是否正当的情况下就发货了。这些片段加在一起，足以多次制造出该病毒。至关重要的是，在埃斯维尔特的叙述中，利用现代工具对已知病毒进行逆向工程并不需要顶尖技能。任何一个普通的生物学研究生都可能胜任。而人工智能可能正在让这种基础的病毒工程变得更加容易。理论上，聊天机器人可以帮助你策划一场生物武器袭击，就像它能指导你修理洗碗机一样：通过找到并整合互联网上浩瀚的信息宝库，提供逐步操作指南以应对陌生的挑战，并解答随后可能出现的所有疑难问题。而且有证据表明，人工智能模型确实会为潜在的生物恐怖分子提供这类协助。在2023年的一项研究中，麻省理工学院的研究人员让学生向当时的聊天机器人寻求关于制造一场大流行的指导。不到一小时，这些人工智能模型就建议了四种有前景的病原体，提供了用合成DNA制造它们的详细方案，列出了一批筛查标准较低的DNA合成零售商，并建议说——如果用户即便有这些帮助仍然无法制造出病毒——他们可以购买合同研究组织的协助，让其代为完成部分生物工程工作。当然，自2023年以来，前沿模型已经进步了很多。去年，埃斯维尔特创立的生物安全非营利组织SecureBio发现，一个OpenAI模型在解决复杂实验室问题的故障排除方面，表现超过了94%的病毒学专家。Anthropic的内部研究也得出了类似结果。在一项实验中，该公司让非专业人士起草一份生物武器获取计划。它给一些参与者提供了基础互联网资源，给另一些参与者提供了Claude模型的协助（关闭了安全防护措施）。根据那些审查提案中关键错误的生物防御专家所说，借助人工智能工作的参与者制定出的蓝图可行性要高得多。因此，有理由认为，具备从基因组蓝图中逆向工程病毒所需技能和资源的人数正在急剧上升——随之而来的是，一个嗜血的虚无主义者或意识形态狂热分子获得危险病原体的风险也在上升。比这更糟糕的是

##段落
重现天花？埃斯维尔特（Esvelt）的第二个担忧是，这些相同的技术力量——加上顶尖科学家往往不计后果的野心——将导致一种超级病毒的发现或开发，一种新的或定制设计的病原体，比自然界过去出现的任何东西都更危险。如今，一些科学家正积极尝试发现——并公开鉴定——自然界中传播的新型病毒，这些病毒理论上可能引发下一次大流行。另一些人则进行所谓的“功能获得”实验，通过改变病原体来辨别哪些突变会使它们更具传染性、致命性或更难以检测（有人声称新冠疫情正是源于这类研究，尽管这一理论被流行病学家广泛否定）。这项工作通常旨在预判未来的流行病学威胁，以便我们能在它们到来之前开发出疫苗。但他们的工作可能无意中为不法分子提供了逆向工程大规模杀伤性生物武器的配方。此外，基因编辑和人工智能的进步可能带来病毒工程领域的突破，从而产生末日性病原体。斯坦福大学和Arc研究所研究人员最近的一项研究加剧了这种恐惧。科学家们用一种名为“Evo”的人工智能，在噬菌体——感染细菌的简单病毒——的DNA序列上进行了训练。然后，他们用这个“基因组语言模型”生成了数百种自然界中不存在的噬菌体的蓝图。其中16种设计产生了可行的病原体，有些在杀灭细菌方面比它们的天然祖先更有效。然而，明确的是，新型病原体是我们这个物种面临的最大安全威胁之一。理论上，科学家有朝一日可能能够使用相同的基本技术来设计新型人类病毒。更重要的是，即使基因组语言模型无法完成这一任务，它们仍可能帮助用户调整现有病毒，使其更具传染性、致命性或疫苗抗性。这些发现理论上可能流入业余生物恐怖分子或像奥姆真理教这样资金充足的极端组织手中。或者，一个国家支持的武器计划可能开发出一种灾难性的超级病毒，然后通过实验室泄漏或（也许更不可能的是）蓄意的种族灭绝企图将其释放到世界上。前者情景已有先例：苏联曾试图将天花和马尔堡病毒武器化，尽管此类生物武器存在相当大的危险且军事效用存疑。在此过程中，苏联科学家在测试期间意外引发了天花疫情，同时还让炭疽从实验室泄漏，导致至少64人死亡。话虽如此，有理由质疑人工智能是否真的在制造一场同步……

##段落
人工大流行变得更有可能。聊天机器人或许能解决一个怀有灭绝野心、却只有业余生物学水平的人所面临的一些难题，但它未必能清除此人道路上最大的障碍。病毒工程是一项复杂、艰难且依赖实体操作的工作。要成功完成它，需要科学家所称的“隐性知识”——那些难以用语言解释的实践技能与理解：懂得如何抑制可能扯断脆弱DNA链的手部颤抖，懂得如何辨认溶液中的DNA已达到适当浓度，懂得如何凭气味判断样本已被污染。而这些正是Claude仍无法可靠传授的东西。在研究中，能够使用大型语言模型的业余人士，往往在书面生物学挑战上表现更好——但在实际实验室操作中并非如此。在一项2026年的随机研究中，使用前沿AI系统的非科学家，完成多步骤实验室任务的可能性并不比仅依赖互联网的人更高。当然，对于远藤诚一那种类型的有抱负的生物恐怖分子——受过研究生训练、拥有丰富实验室经验的科学家——隐性知识未必是个问题。但至少，聊天机器人似乎并没有把每一个上过AP生物课的不满者都变成合格的病毒学家。而且，尽管AI很可能帮助顶尖生物学家推进其领域的前沿，定制工程化末日病毒的障碍依然巨大。“Evo”实验可以说就是一个例证。尽管该模型确实为几种新型噬菌体生成了可行的蓝图，但它所建议的基因组几乎全部无效。研究人员不得不费力测试数百个DNA序列，才得到16条可存活的链。而在实验室中工程化改造一种极其微小、众所周知、能够感染大肠杆菌的噬菌体的略微修改版本——并创造出一种比自然界迄今所演化出的任何病毒都更可怕的新型病毒——这两件事并不特别相似。打个勉强的比方：我能在NBA 2K26里隔扣维克托·文班亚马，并不意味着我在现实中隔扣他这件事上取得了进展。即便在CRISPR和ChatGPT的时代，生物学仍然是一门异常困难的学科，难以被可靠地建模。修改单个基因的效果往往会带来不可预测且不一致的结果，因宿主生物学、免疫反应以及科学家仅部分了解的环境条件而异。AI或许能帮助我们克服这些复杂性，也可能不能。科学家们对于合成大流行构成的风险有多严重——以及AI在多大程度上放大了这一风险——意见不一。然而，清楚的是，新型病原体是我们这个物种面临的最大安全威胁之一。即便合成……

##段落
基因编辑生物学和人工智能当时尚不存在，自然选择会不断产生新病毒——并周期性地演化出能迷惑人类免疫系统的病毒。因此，无论人工智能对病毒工程有何影响，我们都迫切需要让社会降低对未来大流行病的脆弱性。在一个聊天机器人和CRISPR可能让生物恐怖主义变得更容易的世界里，未能大力投资公共卫生就更加鲁莽了。好消息是，我们从惨痛的经验中已经知道，可以采取许多步骤来降低新大流行病风险，并在需要时做好准备应对。政府可以通过投资能预防整个病毒家族（理想情况下是所有病毒）的疫苗和广谱抗病毒药物，来限制新型传染病的破坏力；通过资助细致的废水和临床监测，提高早期发现疫情的概率；通过开发和储备万无一失的个人防护装备，确保必要工作人员在大流行病期间不必在保命和维持文明运转之间做选择；通过升级通风和过滤系统，让室内空间对空气传播病毒更不友好；通过强制对合成DNA订单进行严格筛查，降低生物恐怖主义威胁。对人类将被超级智能机器毁灭的恐惧，目前正引发媒体关注和政治担忧。这或许有其道理。但我们至少应像关注假想中的机器人对手一样，关注我们物种古老的有机器对手——而且不仅因为前者可能开始教后者新把戏。查看更多：人工智能 创新 政治 科技 用最新的Vox填字游戏让大脑休息一下 不想要孩子的奇怪悲伤 阻止卡玛拉2028的悄然运动正愈演愈烈 一个家伙做了一个深度伪造应用，把女性照片变成裸照。结果不太妙。 为什么特朗普的拉丁裔选民正在远离他 播客 电子邮件（必填） 注册 提交您的电子邮件，即表示您同意我们的条款和隐私声明。本网站受reCAPTCHA和谷歌隐私政策及服务条款保护。广告商内容来自 这是原生广告的标题

readings.title: Let’s stop calling them “soft skills” — and call them “real skills” instead
body: Let’s stop calling them “soft skills” — and call them “real skills” instead
We persist in hiring and training as if we’re running a bowling squad, as if easily measured skills are all that matter.

What causes successful organizations to fail ? What makes stocks fade, innovations slow, customers jump ship? We can agree that certain skills are essential. That hiring coders who can’t code, salespeople who can’t sell, or architects who can’t design is a waste. But these skills — let’s call them vocational skills — have become the backbone of the recruitment process.

But how do you explain that similar organizations, with similarly vocationally skilled people, find themselves with very different outcomes? Most of the textbooks that students experience and the tests they take are about vocational skills, the checkboxes that have to be checked to get a job. By misdefining “vocational” and focusing on these allegedly essential skills, we’ve diminished the value of the other skills that matter.

We give too little respect to the other skills when we call them “soft” and imply that they’re optional. What actually separates thriving organizations from struggling ones are the difficult-to-measure attitudes, processes and perceptions of the people who do the work.

Vocational skills can be taught: You’re not born knowing engineering or copywriting or even graphic design, therefore they must be something we can teach. But we let ourselves off the hook when it comes to decision-making, eager participation, dancing with fear, speaking with authority, working in teams , seeing the truth, speaking the truth, inspiring others, doing more than we’re asked, caring and being willing to change things. We underinvest in this training, fearful that these things are innate and can’t be taught. Perhaps they’re talents. And so we downplay them, calling them soft skills, making it easy for us to move on to something seemingly more urgent.

At scale, organizations pay less attention to soft skills when hiring because we’ve persuaded ourselves that vocational skills are impersonal and easier to measure. If it’s easier to test for, it seems more important when selecting our team.
And we fire slowly (and retrain rarely) when these skills are missing, because we’re worried about stepping on toes, being called out for getting personal or possibly wasting time on a lost cause.

But these skills can all be learned, as obvious skills like chess or typing can be learned. We learn them accidentally, by osmosis, by the collisions we have with teachers, parents, bosses and the world. Even though they’re more difficult to measure, that doesn’t mean we can’t improve them, can’t practice them or can’t change the way we do our work.

Let’s stop calling them soft. They’re interpersonal skills. Leadership skills. The skills of charisma and diligence and contribution. But these modifiers, while accurate, somehow edge them away from the vocational skills, the skills that we actually hire for, the skills we measure a graduate degree on.
So let’s uncomfortably call them real skills instead.
Real because they work, because they’re at the heart of what we need today.
Real because even if you’ve got the vocational skills, you’re no help to us without these human skills, the things that we can’t write down or program a computer to do.
Real skills can’t replace vocational skills, of course. What they can do is amplify the things you’ve already been measuring.
Imagine a team member with all the traditional vocational skills: productive, skilled, experienced. A resume that can prove it. That’s a fine baseline.

Now add to it. Perceptive, charismatic, driven, focused, goal-setting, inspiring and motivated. Generous, empathic and consistent. A deep listener , with patience. What happens to your organization when someone like that joins your team?
Writing in the Harvard Business Review , Lou Solomon reports that 69 percent of managers are uncomfortable communicating with their employees. I’d guess that many of the other 31 percent are lying.

Communicating with employees is uncomfortable because we’ve built systems of compliance and dominance that make it difficult. We ask people to leave their humanity at the door, then use authority to change behavior. We overlay corporate greed and short-term thinking with a human desire to create work that matters.

How do we build people-centric organizations while also accepting the fact that two thirds of our managers (presumably well paid, well trained and integral to our success) are so uncomfortable doing an essential part of their job that they admitted it to a stranger?

In a recent survey, the Graduate Management Admission Council reported that although MBAs were strong in analytical aptitude, quantitative expertise and information-gathering ability, they were sorely lacking in other critical areas that employers find equally attractive: strategic thinking, written and oral communication, leadership and adaptability . Are these mutually exclusive? Must we trade one for the other?

The foundation of all real skills is this one: the confidence and permission to talk to one another. Not to manage, belittle, intimidate or control. Simply to seek to be understood and to do the work to understand.

Excerpted from The Song of Significance: A New Manifesto for Teams by Seth Godin, in agreement with Portfolio, an imprint of Penguin Publishing Group, a division of Penguin Random House LLC. Copyright © Seth Godin 2023.

about work. His books have been translated into 38 languages. Godin writes one of the most popular marketing blogs in the world, and his TED talks are among the most popular of all time. He is the founder of the altMBA, the social media pioneer Squidoo, and Yoyodyne, one of the first internet companies. Find out more at seths.blog.

##段落
我们不要再称它们为“软技能”了——而应称之为“真正的技能”。

##段落
2023年6月9日

##段落
/ Seth Godin

##段落
Facebook X LinkedIn Reddit WhatsApp

##段落
Debora Szpilman

##段落
我们坚持用管理保龄球队的方式来招聘和培训，仿佛容易量化的技能就是一切。

##段落
是什么导致成功的组织走向失败？是什么让股票褪色、创新放缓、客户流失？我们可以认同某些技能至关重要。招聘不会编程的程序员、不会销售的销售员、不会设计的建筑师，纯属浪费。但这些技能——我们姑且称之为职业技能——已经成为招聘流程的支柱。

##段落
但你怎么解释，条件相似的组织、拥有职业技能相似的人才，却得到截然不同的结果？学生所接触的大多数教科书和参加的考试都是关于职业技能的，是求职时必须勾选的复选框。通过错误地定义“职业”并聚焦于这些所谓的基本技能，我们贬低了其他重要技能的价值。

##段落
当我们把其他技能称为“软”技能并暗示它们是可有可无的时，我们给予了它们太少的尊重。真正区分蓬勃发展的组织与苦苦挣扎的组织，是那些从事具体工作的人的难以衡量的态度、流程和认知。

##段落
职业技能是可以教授的：你不是天生就懂工程或文案写作，甚至平面设计，因此它们必然是我们能够传授的东西。但在决策、积极投入、与恐惧共舞、有权威地表达、团队协作、看清真相、说出真相、激励他人、超越职责地付出、关心并愿意改变现状这些方面，我们却放任自流。我们对这些培训投入不足，担心这些东西是天生的、无法教授。也许它们是天赋。于是我们贬低它们，称之为软技能，让我们轻易转向看似更紧迫的事情。

##段落
在组织层面，招聘时对软技能关注较少，因为我们说服自己职业技能是客观的、更容易衡量的。如果更容易测试，在挑选团队时就显得更重要。

##段落
而当这些技能缺失时，我们解雇得很慢（也很少再培训），因为我们担心得罪人、被指责针对个人，或者可能在注定失败的事情上浪费时间。

##段落
但这些技能都是可以习得的，就像 chess 或打字等显而易见的技能可以习得一样。我们在不经意间学习它们——通过潜移默化，通过与老师、父母、老板和世界的碰撞。尽管它们更难衡量，但这并不意味着我们不能改进它们、不能练习它们。

##段落
他们无法改变我们的工作方式。
##段落
我们当然能改变。
##段落
让我们别再称它们为软技能。它们是人际交往能力。领导能力。魅力、勤勉和贡献的能力。但这些修饰词虽然准确，却不知怎地将它们与职业技能——我们真正招聘时看重的技能、我们衡量研究生学位的技能——拉开了距离。
##段落
所以，让我们别扭地称它们为"真实技能"吧。
##段落
真实，因为它们管用，因为它们是我们当今所需的核心。
##段落
真实，因为即使你拥有职业技能，若缺乏这些人类技能——那些我们无法写下来、无法编程让计算机去做的事——你对我们也没有帮助。
##段落
真实技能当然无法取代职业技能。它们能做的是放大你已经在衡量的那些东西。
##段落
想象一位拥有所有传统职业技能的团队成员：高效、专业、经验丰富。一份能证明这一切的简历。这是一个不错的基本线。
##段落
现在往上加。敏锐、有魅力、有驱动力、专注、善于设定目标、鼓舞人心且自我驱动。慷慨、有同理心且始终如一。一个深度的倾听者，有耐心。当这样的人加入你的团队时，你的组织会发生什么？
##段落
卢·所罗门在《哈佛商业评论》中写道，69%的管理者与员工沟通时感到不自在。我猜另外31%里有很多人在撒谎。
##段落
与员工沟通之所以不自在，是因为我们建立的合规与支配体系让沟通变得困难。我们要求人们把人性留在门外，然后用权威去改变行为。我们用人类对创造有意义工作的渴望，去掩盖企业的贪婪和短视思维。
##段落
我们如何构建以人为本的组织，同时接受这样一个事实：我们三分之二的管理者（想必薪酬优厚、训练有素、对我们的成功不可或缺）对工作中一个必不可少的环节如此不自在，以至于他们向一个陌生人坦承了这一点？
##段落
在最近一项调查中，管理专业研究生入学委员会报告称，尽管MBA在分析能力、量化专长和信息收集能力方面表现强劲，但他们在雇主同样看重的其他关键领域严重欠缺：战略思维、书面与口头沟通、领导力和适应能力。这些是互斥的吗？我们必须以一换一吗？
##段落
所有真实技能的基础是这一条：彼此交谈的信心与许可。不是为了管理、贬低、恐吓或控制。只是为了寻求被理解，并付出努力去理解。
##段落
摘自塞斯·高汀的《意义之歌：团队新宣言》，经Portfolio（企鹅出版集团旗下品牌，企鹅兰登书屋的一个部门）授权。
